text: Last lesson built the server side of the bridge, a Script Include called FreezeWindowChecker with a public method named checkDateRange. This lesson writes the client script that actually calls it, and covers the real, standard pattern you'll use every time you call GlideAjax from here forward.

You start by constructing a new GlideAjax object, naming the Script Include exactly as its type property is defined. Then sysparm_name is special - it's the one reserved parameter that always tells GlideAjax which public method on that Script Include to actually run. Every other parameter name you choose becomes an argument, read on the server with getParameter using that exact same name.

getXMLAnswer is the real, standard way to receive the result, and it is asynchronous. It does not hand back the server's answer as a return value - instead, you give it a callback function, and that function only runs later, once the server has actually processed the request and responded.

Here's the mistake that trips almost everyone up at least once: storing the answer in an outside variable, then checking that variable immediately on the next line. That check runs before the server ever responds, so the variable is still undefined at that exact moment - the message never fires, even when the real server-side answer would have been true.

The fix is always the same: do the checking, and any g_form update, inside the callback function itself. That's the only place in your code where you can be sure the server has actually answered. Build the call, pass getXMLAnswer a callback, and put all of your logic inside that callback.

You now have both halves of a full GlideAjax round trip: a Script Include extending AbstractAjaxProcessor, and a client script calling it correctly and asynchronously. Next lesson's lab puts both halves together into one complete, working scenario: catching change freeze conflicts as a user types new dates.
